questions.description: Nature's pincushion, and it never asked to be hugged.
questions.question: Look at this porcupine. What are its sharp quills really?
hints: The quills grow out of its skin, like the rest of its coat.
They are made of keratin, the same stuff as your fingernails.
Next to the quills, the porcupine also has a soft coat of fur.
questions.fun_fact: A North American porcupine can have about 30,000 quills, and each lost quill grows back.

media.credit: Thomas Quine · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Thomas Quine

questions.description: A nose on top of the head: perfect for breathing, terrible for wearing glasses.
questions.question: It sits on top of the head, opens to breathe air and shuts tight underwater. Which animals breathe through a blowhole?
hints: These animals are mammals that never leave the water.
When they breathe out, a spray of mist shoots into the air.
The biggest animal on Earth is one of them.
questions.fun_fact: Whales with teeth have one blowhole, but baleen whales, like the humpback, have two.

media.credit: Pattaya Patrol from Pattaya · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Pattaya Patrol from Pattaya

questions.description: Hide and seek champion of the forest, and it's not even trying.
questions.question: Look closely at this green “leaf”. What kind of animal is it really?
hints: Count its legs.
It has six legs.
Its relatives include stick insects, which look like twigs.
questions.fun_fact: Some leaf insects even sway from side to side when they walk, like a leaf in the wind.

media.credit: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Bernard DUPONT from FRANCE

questions.description: This swimmer never complains that the water is too cold.
questions.question: I can't fly in the sky, but I flap my stiff wings to “fly” underwater. I live mostly in the southern half of the world. Who am I?
hints: I'm a bird.
I wear black and white, like a tuxedo.
Many of my kind live around Antarctica.
questions.fun_fact: The gentoo penguin can swim at about 35 km/h (22 mph), faster than any other diving bird.

media.credit: Erwan AMICE · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Erwan AMICE

questions.description: Yoga in the desert at sunrise: very healthy, and very practical.
questions.question: On foggy mornings in the Namib Desert, this beetle stands on its head with its back to the wind. Why?
questions.answer: To catch water from the fog
wrong_answers: To lay eggs in the sand
hints: It almost never rains where this beetle lives.
Fog rolls in from the sea and leaves tiny drops on its body.
The drops run down its back straight into its mouth.
questions.fun_fact: Engineers have studied these beetles to design materials that collect drinking water from fog.

media.credit: Didier Descouens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Didier Descouens

questions.description: Two giant teeth, and not a single visit to the dentist.
questions.question: A walrus has two long tusks, which are giant teeth that grow up to about 1 m (3 ft). What does it often use them for?
questions.answer: To pull itself onto the ice
hints: A walrus is very heavy and clumsy out of the water.
Think about climbing out of a swimming pool with no ladder.
It hooks them into the edge of the ice, like ice picks.
questions.fun_fact: The walrus's scientific name means “tooth-walker”, because it uses its tusks to haul itself along.

media.credit: AWeith · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: AWeith

questions.description: Some scientists use microscopes; this one used good manners and a lot of patience.
questions.question: From 1967, Dian Fossey studied wild mountain gorillas in the misty volcanoes of Rwanda. How did she get them to accept her nearby?
questions.answer: She copied their eating, grooming and soft grunts
wrong_answers: She left out bananas for them every day
She watched only from a hidden tent
hints: Gorillas feel safest around someone who behaves like one of them.
She spent months sitting quietly out in the open near the groups, so they could see her and get used to her.
She acted like a gorilla, but without dressing up as one.
questions.fun_fact: Fossey's book “Gorillas in the Mist” became a 1988 film starring Sigourney Weaver.

media.credit: MONUSCO Photos · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MONUSCO Photos

questions.description: A monkey whose face looks like a toddler got hold of a brand-new set of crayons.
questions.question: Mandrills live in the rainforests of Central Africa. How many of them can travel together in one group?
hints: Mandrill groups are among the biggest of any monkey.
Scientists call these huge groups “hordes”.
Counting them can take ages: think big, but not a whole city.
questions.fun_fact: The male mandrill is the largest monkey in the world, and his face gets brighter when he is the boss.

media.credit: Hans Hillewaert · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Hans Hillewaert

questions.description: A frog that treats winter like the freezer section and comes out fresh in spring.
questions.question: The wood frog of North America survives winter frozen, with no heartbeat. Before it freezes, its liver floods its cells with what kind of substance to protect them?
hints: The substance works a bit like antifreeze in a car.
Your own blood carries the same thing, which gives you energy.
It's the same kind of substance that makes sweets taste sweet.
questions.fun_fact: A frozen wood frog can have about two-thirds of the water in its body turned to ice.

media.credit: ForestWander · CC BY-SA 3.0 us · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ForestWander

questions.description: Every mouse in the neighborhood has this bird's picture on a “most wanted” poster.
questions.question: This bird has a white, heart-shaped face, flies almost without a sound, and can catch a mouse in total darkness just by hearing it. Which bird is it?
hints: It hunts at night.
Its heart-shaped face collects sounds like a satellite dish.
It often nests in old farm buildings.
questions.fun_fact: A barn owl's ears are at different heights, which helps it tell exactly where a sound comes from.

media.credit: Николай Максимович · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Николай Максимович

questions.description: Someone in the garage has been knitting, and it wasn't Grandma.
questions.question: You find a sticky net in the corner of the garage, with a fly stuck in it. Which animal made it?
hints: The builder waits for its dinner to fly in.
It makes thread from its own body.
It has eight legs.
questions.fun_fact: Spider silk is stronger than a steel thread of the same thickness.

media.credit: Farhan Sazid · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Farhan Sazid

questions.description: A whole troop of loud neighbors who never knock before borrowing your snacks.
questions.question: Baboons live in big troops in Africa, walk on all fours across the savanna, and have a tail. Which group of animals are they?
hints: They are primates, like us.
Gorillas and chimpanzees have no tail, and baboons do.
Lemurs live only on Madagascar.
questions.fun_fact: Baboons often sleep high on cliffs or in tall trees to stay safe at night.

media.credit: Kev Moses · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Kev Moses

questions.description: The world's most crowded winter holiday, and every guest is orange.
questions.question: Look: in winter, millions of monarch butterflies pack together on trees like these. Why do they do it?
hints: The forests they choose are high in the mountains.
Butterflies can't fly when they get too cold.
It's like penguins huddling in a storm.
questions.fun_fact: Monarchs return to the same forests each winter, even though none of them has ever been there before.

media.credit: Charles J. Sharp · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Charles J. Sharp

questions.description: A physicist who made energy come in bite-sized portions.
questions.question: “In 1900, to explain the glow of hot objects, I said energy comes in tiny packets. The constant h is named after me.” Who am I?
hints: I was German, and I started quantum physics without really meaning to.
A big German research society and an ESA space telescope are named after me.
My surname sounds like a long piece of wood.
questions.fun_fact: Planck later called his idea of energy packets “an act of desperation”. He had no other way to make the math work.

media.credit: Hi-Res Images of · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author:
Hi-Res Images of

Chemical Elements

questions.description: A temperature scale too cool to wear the little circle.
questions.question: This temperature unit is named after a 19th-century British lord, starts at absolute zero and never uses the word “degree”. Which is it?
hints: Scientists use it more than weather reports do.
Water freezes at about 273 of these.
The lord took his title from a river in Glasgow.
questions.fun_fact: William Thomson became Lord Kelvin, naming himself after the River Kelvin, which flows past the University of Glasgow.

media.credit: PointsofNoReturn · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: PointsofNoReturn

questions.description: A heavy element with a seriously heavy job.
questions.question: It fuels most nuclear power plants, is named after a planet found eight years earlier, and has the heaviest atoms found in large amounts in nature. Which element is it?
hints: Its number on the periodic table is 92.
The planet it is named after was discovered in 1781.
That planet is the seventh from the Sun.
questions.fun_fact: A uranium fuel pellet the size of a fingertip can give about as much energy as a ton of coal.

media.credit: Christian David · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Christian David

questions.description: Electrons used to orbit like planets until someone made them fuzzy.
questions.question: “In 1926 I wrote the wave equation that turned electron orbits into fuzzy clouds of probability.” Who am I?
hints: I was Austrian and won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1933.
The basic equation of quantum mechanics carries my name.
I am famous for a thought experiment about a cat in a box.
questions.fun_fact: Schrödinger came up with his famous cat in 1935 to show how strange quantum theory seemed, not to praise it.

media.credit: Geek3 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Geek3

questions.description: Physicists bet on black holes, and somebody had to pay up.
questions.question: Hawking bet that information swallowed by a black hole is lost forever. In 2004 he admitted defeat at a conference. In which city?
hints: It was not the city where he worked.
The conference was in a European capital.
The city is famous for James Joyce and the River Liffey.
questions.fun_fact: Hawking paid physicist John Preskill with a baseball encyclopedia, a book from which information can be got back easily.

media.credit: Event Horizon Telescope · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Event Horizon Telescope

questions.description: A giant underground bathtub that nobody is allowed to swim in.
questions.question: “I led the team at Super-Kamiokande that showed in 1998 that neutrinos change type, so they have mass. I shared the 2015 Nobel Prize.” Who am I?
hints: I am Japanese, and my Nobel Prize was in physics.
I shared the prize with the Canadian Arthur McDonald.
My teacher won a Nobel Prize in 2002 for the earlier Kamiokande detector.
questions.fun_fact: Super-Kamiokande is a tank of 50,000 tons of ultra-pure water, 1,000 m underground and lined with about 11,000 light sensors.

media.credit: Motokoka · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Motokoka

questions.description: Humanity, vacuum-packed for easy storage.
questions.question: Atoms are almost entirely empty space. If you squeezed all the empty space out of every person on Earth, what would all of humanity fit into?
hints: The answer is much smaller than you'd think.
Almost all of an atom's mass sits in a nucleus about 100,000 times smaller than the atom.
You could hold it between two fingers.
questions.fun_fact: If an atom were as big as a sports stadium, its nucleus would be about the size of a pea in the middle.

media.credit: No restrictions · Wikimedia Commons

questions.description: Some scientists travel halfway around the world just to be in the dark for five minutes.
questions.question: In 1919 Arthur Eddington sailed to the island of Príncipe to photograph stars near the Sun during a total eclipse. What did he want to show?
wrong_answers: That the Moon has no air
That the Sun is made of iron
That light slows down in space
hints: He was testing a new theory published a few years earlier.
The stars seemed to sit in slightly the wrong places.
The theory was Einstein's general relativity.
questions.fun_fact: When the results were announced in November 1919, newspapers around the world made Einstein famous almost overnight.

media.credit: J.A. Lunn · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: J.A. Lunn

questions.description: Splitting hairs, but on an atomic level.
questions.question: You pull out one of your hairs and look at its width. About how many atoms lined up side by side would stretch across it?
hints: A hair is less than a tenth of a millimeter thick.
An atom is about a tenth of a billionth of a meter across.
The answer is somewhere near half a million.
questions.fun_fact: Gold leaf can be hammered so thin that it is only a few hundred atoms thick.

media.credit: Чуликова · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Чуликова

questions.description: A proton's evil twin, minus the mustache.
questions.question: The antiproton was discovered in 1955. It has the same mass as a proton but a negative charge. What is it made of?
hints: A normal proton is made of three smaller particles.
Turn everything inside the proton into antimatter.
Two anti-up and one anti-down.
questions.fun_fact: When an antiproton meets a proton, both disappear in a flash of energy, turning their mass into energy as in E = mc².

media.credit: Milkodromeda · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Milkodromeda

questions.description: The barnyard's toughest gear, and no farm animal ever had to buy it in a shop.
questions.question: I'm hard and made of the same stuff as your fingernails. Horses, cows and goats walk on me all day. What am I?
hints: You find me at the bottom of an animal's legs.
Blacksmiths sometimes nail metal shoes onto me.
I go “clip-clop” on a hard road.
questions.fun_fact: A horse really walks on the tip of a single toe: its hoof is like one giant toenail.

media.credit: SharonPapierdreams · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: SharonPapierdreams

questions.description: Headgear that gets thrown away and grown again every single year.
questions.question: Thousands of years ago, people carved tools and combs from deer antlers. What are antlers made of?
hints: It's the same material as something inside your own body.
While they grow, antlers are covered in soft, furry skin full of blood.
You have 206 of these inside you.
questions.fun_fact: Antlers fall off and grow back every year, and a moose's antlers can grow about 2.5 cm (1 in) in a single day.

media.credit: shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: shankar s. from Dubai, united arab emirates

questions.description: When your body decides a harmless snack is public enemy number one.
questions.question: Hives, which doctors call urticaria, often come from an allergy. What are they?
questions.answer: Itchy raised welts on the skin
hints: Brushing against a stinging nettle can cause them.
They are pink or red and can move around the body.
They itch a lot and often fade within a day.
questions.fun_fact: Hives don't only come from allergies: cold, heat or even pressure on the skin can set them off in some people.

media.credit: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Dominicus Johannes Bergsma

questions.description: Proof that stairs have been fighting humans for centuries.
questions.question: You twist your foot the wrong way, your ankle swells and turns blue, and the doctor calls it a sprain. What got stretched or torn?
hints: A sprain is not a break.
These tough bands hold your joints together.
They join one bone to another bone.
questions.fun_fact: The ankle is one of the most often sprained joints in the body, especially in sports with jumping and quick turns.

media.credit: Ben Schumin from Montgomery Village, Maryland, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ben Schumin from Montgomery Village, Maryland, USA

questions.description: The joint that lets you wave, throw and pretend to be a windmill.
questions.question: Your shoulder lets your arm swing in a full circle and is your body's most movable joint. What kind of joint is it?
hints: Your elbow can only bend one way; the shoulder is very different.
Your hip is the same kind of joint.
A round end sits in a shallow cup.
questions.fun_fact: The shoulder's socket is so shallow that it's often compared to a golf ball sitting on a tee.

media.credit: Isiwal · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Isiwal

questions.description: The body's built-in fruit bowl, minus the fruit.
questions.question: Its name is Latin for “basin,” it's shaped like a bowl, and your legs join your body there. What is this group of bones called?
hints: It's in the lower half of your body.
You put your hands on it when you stand with hands on hips.
Your hip bones are part of it.
questions.fun_fact: Scientists can often tell whether a skeleton belonged to a man or a woman just by looking at its pelvis.

media.credit: Diliff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Diliff

questions.description: Plants wear it every single day and never change their outfit.
questions.question: Two French chemists named it in 1817 from two Greek words, and it makes plants green. What does “chlorophyll” mean?
hints: The first part is also in “chlorine”, a pale yellow-green gas.
Thin Greek “phyllo” pastry gets its name from the same word as the second part.
Think of the greenest part of most plants.
questions.fun_fact: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light but reflects green, which is why leaves look green to us.

media.credit: Akshaya govindasamy · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Akshaya govindasamy

questions.description: The brain's longest delivery route, and it never asks for directions.
questions.question: It's the long, thin part of a neuron, carries the signal away from the cell body, and in your leg can be about 1 m (3 ft) long. What is it?
hints: A neuron has many short branches, but usually only one of these.
It's often wrapped in a fatty coating that speeds up the signal.
Its name comes from the Greek word for “axis”.
questions.fun_fact: The squid's giant axon is up to about 1 mm thick, which let scientists in the 1950s first record how nerve signals work.

media.credit: ZEISS Microscopy from Germany · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: ZEISS Microscopy from Germany

questions.description: Some cheeks come with built-in parking spots for smiles.
questions.question: I knew you before you were born. You got half your genes from me, and maybe the little dents in your cheeks when you smile. Who am I?
hints: I'm part of your family.
You might have my eye color too.
I'm one of the two people your genes came from.
questions.fun_fact: Dimples often come from a cheek muscle that is a little shorter or split in two, and some children's dimples fade as they grow.

media.credit: Masum-al-hasan · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Masum-al-hasan

questions.description: Proof that even great scientists doodle in their notebooks.
questions.question: In 1837 Darwin sketched it in a notebook under the words “I think”. It shows how species split off from shared ancestors. What is it?
hints: It sums up the big idea Darwin worked out after his voyage on the Beagle.
Every living thing sits somewhere on it.
Humans and chimpanzees sit on two twigs of the same branch.
questions.fun_fact: The only illustration in Darwin's 1859 book “On the Origin of Species” is a branching diagram of this kind.

media.credit: Elliott & Fry · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Elliott & Fry

questions.description: The only math problem where numbers grow by splitting up.
questions.question: An embryo starts as a single cell. If every cell splits in two, four times over, how many cells are there?
hints: After the first split there are 2 cells.
After the second split there are 4.
Keep doubling: 2, 4, 8…
questions.fun_fact: The first baby conceived by IVF, where the embryo's first cell splits happen in a lab dish, was Louise Brown, born in England in 1978.

media.credit: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya

questions.description: Gregor Mendel ate his way through a lot of peas so you could answer this.
questions.question: In Mendel's peas, purple flowers, round seeds and tall stems were all “dominant”. What does a dominant trait do?
questions.answer: Shows up even with just one copy of the gene
wrong_answers: Skips every other generation of the family
Grows stronger as the plant gets older
Shows up only in the plants that are male
hints: Its opposite is called “recessive”.
A cross of purple and white plants still gave only purple flowers.
One version of the gene is enough to hide the other.
questions.fun_fact: Mendel grew about 28,000 pea plants in his monastery garden in what is now the Czech Republic.

media.credit: Forest & Kim Starr · CC BY 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Forest & Kim Starr

questions.description: Getting to the end of this question is the whole point.
questions.question: Every chromosome has one at each tip, they shrink a little each time a cell divides, and they earned a 2009 Nobel Prize. What are they?
hints: Their name comes from Greek words meaning “end part”.
They protect the chromosome a bit like the plastic tips on shoelaces.
Their name starts with “telo-”.
questions.fun_fact: Telomerase, the enzyme that rebuilds telomeres, was found on Christmas Day 1984 by Carol Greider, then a student in Elizabeth Blackburn's lab.

media.credit: Korinna · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Korinna

questions.description: Your parents passed you their eyes, their nose and, apparently, their blood paperwork.
questions.question: Blood types A, B, AB and O all come from one gene. How many common versions (alleles) of that gene make all four?
hints: Each person carries two versions of the gene, one from each parent.
Type AB means you got two different versions.
Look at the letters in the blood type names.
questions.fun_fact: Type O is the most common blood type in the world.

media.credit: CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Ufficio Comunicazione, Azienda Ospedaliera SS. Antonio e Biagio e Cesare Arrigo, Alessandria, Biblioteca Biomedica Centro di Documentazione

questions.description: The only question where sticking your tongue out is allowed.
questions.question: Try it now: can you curl your tongue into a tube? About how many people in the world can?
hints: Not everyone can do it.
In a typical classroom, a lot of your classmates can probably do it.
So: most people, but far from all.
questions.fun_fact: Tongue rolling was once taught as a simple inherited trait, but identical twins can differ, so it isn't only genes.

media.credit: Gideon Tsang from Austin, USA · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Gideon Tsang from Austin, USA

questions.description: Collecting Nobel Prizes is a hobby only a handful of people have.
questions.question: Which British biochemist won two Nobel Prizes in Chemistry, first for the structure of insulin, then for a way to read DNA?
hints: He worked in Cambridge, England.
His DNA-reading method was used for the Human Genome Project.
The method is named after him: “… sequencing”.
questions.fun_fact: He turned down a knighthood because he didn't want to be called “Sir”.

media.credit: John Crawford (Photographer) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: John Crawford (Photographer)

questions.description: The tic-tac-toe board of biology class has a famous owner.
questions.question: Biology students predict a cross of one trait with a grid of four boxes. Whose name does that grid carry?
hints: He worked in Cambridge in the early 1900s.
He also bred chickens and sweet peas.
The grid is called a “… square”.
questions.fun_fact: Punnett helped create the Cambridge Barred chicken, whose chicks can be sorted into male and female by their color at hatching.

media.credit: Colin Smith · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Colin Smith

questions.description: Nature's talent show, where the prize is grandchildren.
questions.question: I have no eyes and no plan, yet I decide who has babies. The best-suited survive and pass on their traits. I made moths darker in sooty cities. What am I?
hints: Charles Darwin made me famous in 1859.
Farmers do something similar on purpose when they breed cows.
Unlike dog breeding, no human does the choosing.
questions.fun_fact: Near English factory cities, dark peppered moths went from rare to almost all of them in about 50 years in the 1800s.

media.credit: MicrocosmicWorld · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: MicrocosmicWorld

questions.description: The cell's version of everyone lining up for the class photo.
questions.question: This cell is in metaphase, a stage of cell division. What are the structures lined up across its middle?
hints: They carry your DNA.
Humans have 46 of them in most cells.
Just before the split, they look like little X shapes.
questions.fun_fact: Each chromosome copies itself before the cell divides, which is why it looks like an X at this stage.

media.credit: Natalierussell77 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Natalierussell77

questions.description: A rock that took the long way to get to your backyard.
questions.question: You pick up a meteorite. It feels much heavier than a normal rock and sticks to a magnet. Which metal is it mostly made of?
hints: It is not a precious metal.
The center of the Earth is mostly made of it too.
Leave it out in the rain on Earth and it can rust.
questions.fun_fact: The biggest meteorite ever found, the Hoba meteorite in Namibia, weighs about 60 tonnes and is so heavy it has never been moved.

media.credit: Didier Descouens · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Didier Descouens

questions.description: A metal that went from total nuisance to the top of the charts.
questions.question: Spanish explorers in South America found me mixed with their gold and thought I was a nuisance. Now I'm rarer than gold, and hit albums are named after me. What am I?
hints: I am a precious metal used in expensive rings.
A record that sells even more than a “gold” record is named after me.
I'm a grayish-white metal, and cars use me in their catalytic converters to clean the exhaust.
questions.fun_fact: Until 2019, the official kilogram for the whole world was a small cylinder of platinum and iridium kept in a vault near Paris.

media.credit: Vasyatka1 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Vasyatka1

questions.description: The metal that will happily be hammered flat and never complain.
questions.question: Gold can be hammered into gold leaf thinner than a hair, and it never rusts. Which of these words does NOT describe gold?
hints: Three of these words are about how easily gold changes shape or how it stays shiny.
Think about what happens if you hold a fridge magnet near a gold ring.
Iron and nickel have this property, gold does not.
questions.fun_fact: Gold leaf can be so thin that light shines through it, and it then looks green instead of gold.

media.credit: brandbook.de · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: brandbook.de

questions.description: The man who was so sure of himself he left empty seats for guests who hadn't been born yet.
questions.question: In 1869, which Russian chemist arranged the elements in a table and left gaps for elements nobody had discovered yet?
hints: The table he made hangs in almost every chemistry classroom.
He predicted gallium years before anyone found it.
Element number 101, mendelevium, is named after him.
questions.fun_fact: Mendeleev's predicted “eka-aluminum” was found in 1875 and named gallium, and it matched his guesses almost exactly.

media.credit: Sandbh · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Sandbh

questions.description: Nature's own pincushion, minus the pins.
questions.question: These silvery, needle-like crystals are stibnite. It is the main ore of which element?
hints: The element's chemical symbol comes from the Latin name of this mineral.
It's a brittle metalloid that used to be added to lead to make old printing type harder.
Ancient peoples ground this mineral into a black powder to line their eyes.
questions.fun_fact: Around the ancient Mediterranean and in the Middle East, powdered stibnite was used as black eye makeup (kohl), and its Latin name “stibium” gives antimony its symbol Sb.

media.credit: Robert M. Lavinsky · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Robert M. Lavinsky

questions.description: A metal so rare that one country's bad week can empty jewelers' pockets everywhere.
questions.question: Rhodium makes white gold jewelry shine and cleans car exhaust, and most of it comes from one country. When mines there close, its price jumps. Which country?
hints: The same mines produce most of the world's platinum.
The country is famous for having some of the deepest mines on Earth.
It's at the southern tip of Africa.
questions.fun_fact: In 2021, rhodium cost more than ten times as much as gold.

media.credit: Mauro Cateb · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
media.author: Mauro Cateb

questions.description: Sunshine is free, but most of it doesn't make it into the socket.
questions.question: About how much of the sunlight hitting a normal rooftop solar panel does it turn into electricity?
hints: Most of the sunlight is lost, mostly as heat.
Far more than plants get from sunlight, but well under half.

hints: Mega- also shows up in megawatt and megabyte.
It's more than the number of people living in most big cities.
Mega- stands for a 1 followed by six zeros.
questions.fun_fact: “Mega” comes from the Greek word “megas”, meaning “great”.

questions.description: A unit for when your legs start asking “are we there yet?”
questions.question: How many meters make one kilometer?
hints: It's more than a 100-meter sprint race.
Kilo- is the same start as in kilogram.
It's ten times one hundred.
questions.fun_fact: A marathon is just over 42 kilometers (26.2 miles) long.

questions.description: Someone is getting older, and the candles are doing the math.
questions.question: Look at the candles on this birthday cake. How many decades old is the birthday person?
hints: A decade is a group of years, the way a dozen is a group of eggs.
Decathletes compete in ten events.
One decade is ten years.
questions.fun_fact: The word “decade” comes from the Greek “deka”, meaning ten.

questions.description: The one night a year your bed gets robbed of an hour.
questions.question: Whole countries first moved their clocks forward for summer to save coal during a war. In which year?
hints: Cars were still rare, but electric light was spreading.
Germany was the first country to do it.
It happened during the First World War.
questions.fun_fact: In 1784, Benjamin Franklin joked that Parisians could save candles by simply getting up earlier.

questions.description: A temperature scale that makes the weather report sound like a math test.
questions.question: On Daniel Fahrenheit's scale, a healthy body is about 98.6 degrees and water boils at 212. What does plain water turn into at 32 °F?
hints: 32 is a lot lower than 212.
It's far colder than your body.
On the Celsius scale, this point is exactly 0.
questions.fun_fact: At −40 degrees, the Fahrenheit and Celsius scales show exactly the same number.

questions.description: Blink and you'll miss it, but this gadget won't.
questions.question: The world's fastest runners sprint 100 meters. About how long do the best ones take?
hints: It's much less than a minute.
It's shorter than brushing your teeth, but longer than a sneeze.
Count slowly from one to ten.
questions.fun_fact: In 2009, Usain Bolt ran 100 meters in 9.58 seconds.
